blocks.text: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation of much shorter wavelength, about 10^-10 m. To observe diffraction, the grating spacing must be of the order of the wavelength of the radiation used. The regular array of atoms in a crystal forms a natural diffraction grating with a spacing of typically about 10^-10 m. The scattering of X-rays by the atoms of a crystal lattice gives diffraction effects very like those of visible light on an ordinary grating.

The study of the atomic structure of crystals by X-rays was begun in 1914 by W. H. Bragg and W. L. Bragg. They found that a monochromatic X-ray beam was reflected from a crystal plane as if from a mirror. To understand this, consider a series of atomic planes with constant spacing d parallel to a crystal face (lines PP', P1P1', P2P2' in Fig 15.18). An X-ray beam is incident at an angle theta on the planes. It is reflected from both the upper and lower planes, and the beam reflected from the lower plane travels an extra distance: the path difference between the two reflected beams is 2d sin(theta). For reinforcement this must be a whole number of wavelengths: 2d sin(theta) = n lambda (15.8).

blocks.title: Bragg equation
blocks.text: 2d sin(theta) = n lambda, where d is the spacing of the atomic planes, theta the glancing angle between the X-rays and the planes, and n the order of reflection. If X-rays of known wavelength are diffracted by a crystal, the equation gives the spacing between its parallel planes.

blocks.alt: Three rows of orange atoms a distance d apart, joined by dashed lines. Two blue X-rays come in at angle theta and reflect from the top row and the second row. Red segments mark the extra distance travelled by the lower ray, d sin(theta) on the way in and d sin(theta) on the way out. Text: the extra path is 2d sin(theta); reinforcement when 2d sin(theta) = n lambda (the Bragg equation); used to find d and the structures of haemoglobin and DNA.
blocks.caption: Diffraction of X-rays by a crystal (original diagram after Fig 15.18).
blocks.long_description: The two red segments together make 2d sin(theta). Only at angles where this equals a whole number of wavelengths do the reflections from all the planes add up to a strong beam.

blocks.text: X-ray diffraction has been very useful in finding the structures of biologically important molecules such as haemoglobin, an important constituent of blood, and the double-helix structure of DNA.

X-rays of wavelength 1.54 x 10^-10 m give a first-order reflection from a crystal at a glancing angle of 15.9 degrees. Find the spacing of the planes. Solution: d = n lambda / (2 sin(theta)) = (1)(1.54 x 10^-10) / (2 x 0.274) = 2.81 x 10^-10 m.

blocks.prompt: Why can an ordinary ruled grating not be used to diffract X-rays?
blocks.explanation: Its spacing (about 10^-6 m) is thousands of times larger than X-ray wavelengths (about 10^-10 m), so the angles of diffraction would be far too small; a crystal's atomic spacing matches the X-ray wavelength.

items: X-rays: wavelength about 10^-10 m; crystals act as natural gratings.
Used to find plane spacings and structures (haemoglobin, DNA).
